metadata.title: How Do Websites Know I'm Not a Robot?
metadata.narration_policy: Narration is SCRIPT.md verbatim, one script section per beat. Beat IDs B01-B10 match script sections 1-10; BVDT, BHTF and BOUT are sections 11, 12 and 13. On-screen-only lines (the typed-then-corrected overview, the prompt shown on screen) and source tags in SCRIPT.md are not narrated.
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative graphics only: a grid of drawn traffic-light squares, wavy letters, a checkbox, a 0-to-1 score dial, a stopwatch, a mouse path, a shield. No Google, reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha or Cloudflare logos, no screenshots of real challenge pages, and no copy of any product's widget or colour scheme. Company and product names appear as plain text only where the narration says them. No person icons: 'me' is a cursor. Every example is an illustration, not data; the only figures on screen are those in SCRIPT.md. The Claude composer, verdict page and channel mark are redrawn bookends, not screenshots.

Checked renderable with ./art scenes --check: ClaudeComposerAsk, BrutalistHesitantWriter, ClaudeVerdictArtifact, LogoOutro and their 916 variants. Reused: ClaudeComposerAsk, BrutalistHesitantWriter, ClaudeVerdictArtifact, LogoOutro. Genuine misses (PUNTs): the I'm-not-a-robot checkbox and the stopwatch; no library match for the traffic-light grid, wavy letters, 0-to-1 score dial, behaviour signals or shield, so B02 and B04-B10 are planned as custom Manim scenes. Leads judged from their search descriptions only (files not opened) and rejected: BrandBoondoggleScore (a 0-100 gauge for another film's score table), CursorLayer (a macOS pointer overlay on a real app shell), AlgArtSeedGrid (a generative-art seed grid), BarChart (single-value bars; B08 needs ranges and an under-1-second sliver), CCShell (a Claude Code terminal shell).

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Keya, and this video is about how websites know I'm not a robot. The voice you're hearing is an AI voice reading my script.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hi, Keya'
three result lines land: websites check how you behave, a score instead of a puzzle, traffic lights aren't the whole test
the AI-voice disclosure is spoken while the answered composer holds

props.segment: How Do Websites Know I'm Not a Robot?
props.command: Explain how websites know I'm not a robot.
props.runningText: thinking about checkboxes and traffic lights…
output: Traffic lights aren't the whole test

beats.narration_text: As an automation developer, my bots never ran into a CAPTCHA. But I do, all the time. Click every traffic light. Then every bike. Sometimes two in a row. Why does a website keep asking me to prove I'm human?

shot.visual_intent: A plain 3x3 grid of drawn squares, some holding a simple drawn traffic light (three stacked circles in a rounded box), others a plain shape. A cursor ticks the traffic-light squares one by one on 'Click every traffic light'; the grid refills with bicycle outlines (two circles and a frame) on 'Then every bike'; it refills once more on 'Sometimes two in a row'. A small drawn robot (a square head, two dots, an antenna) glides past a dashed gate without stopping on 'my bots never ran into a CAPTCHA'. The question 'Why does it keep asking me to prove I'm human?' lands last. Everything is a drawn illustration; no logo, no real challenge page.

show.event: a small drawn robot glides straight through a dashed gate on 'my bots never ran into a CAPTCHA'; 'automation developer' reads small above it
the cursor stops at the same gate; a 3x3 grid of drawn squares opens and the cursor ticks every traffic-light square, on 'Click every traffic light'
the grid refills with bicycle outlines and the cursor ticks those, on 'Then every bike'; it refills again on 'Sometimes two in a row'
the question 'Why does a website keep asking me to prove I'm human?' lands under the grid

beats.note: Keya's own experience (tagged in SCRIPT.md). The grid is a drawn illustration, not a copy of any real challenge page. No person icon: 'me' is a cursor.

beats.narration_text: The traffic lights aren't the whole test. More and more, websites also check how you behave, often without you noticing. Let's see how, step by step.

show.event: the writer types 'Prove you can see traffic lights.' in terracotta, finishing before the 50% point
it pauses, then deletes the whole sentence
'Prove you behave like a person.' types in ink
the corrected sentence holds while the voice says 'Let's see how, step by step'

Prove you can see

beats.note: Typed 'Prove you can see traffic lights.' then corrected to 'Prove you behave like a person.' as in SCRIPT.md (on screen only; not narrated). The whole sentence is the trigger phrase so the correction replaces the sentence, not one word. 'Prove you can see traffic lights' is the viewer's likely misconception. Narration lengthened to give the typing room; no lead silence. Verify after render that the correction finishes typing before the 50% frame, and shorten the lines if not.

beats.narration_text: CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. It's a test that checks whether you're a human or a bot. Early versions asked you to read wavy, distorted letters. Today, they come in three main types: text, images and audio.

shot.visual_intent: The word CAPTCHA draws in large; its letters unfold into the long name, one word per letter (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), word by word as spoken. Under it, a plain question card: 'human or bot?'. Then a short row of drawn wavy, distorted letters (a made-up string, not a real challenge) appears with a cursor typing under it, on 'wavy, distorted letters'. Last, three plain drawn cards, 'text', 'images', 'audio' (a letters card, a small picture-grid card and a sound-wave card), land one by one on 'three main types'. Labelled 'illustrative'.

show.event: 'CAPTCHA' lands large; it unfolds letter by letter into the full name as it is spoken
a plain 'human or bot?' card settles under the name on 'checks whether you're a human or a bot'
a row of drawn wavy, distorted letters (made-up, labelled 'illustrative') appears with a text box under it, on 'wavy, distorted letters'
three plain cards land one by one: text, images, audio, on 'text, images and audio'

beats.note: Listen-check CAPTCHA. The letter string is invented for the picture and is not a real challenge. 'Three main types: text, images and audio' is from the Merchant Risk Council post; see FACTCHECK.md. The word 'Today' is the script's own.

beats.narration_text: Then came the "I'm not a robot" checkbox. The click itself isn't the test. Behind it, the system looks at signals like your cookies, your browsing history and your mouse movements. If it's confident you're human, you go straight through. Only if it's unsure does it ask you to pick pictures.

shot.visual_intent: A plain drawn checkbox with the words 'I'm not a robot' beside it (plain text, no logo). A cursor ticks it. The click is shown as small, then pushed aside: behind the box three signal chips slide in, 'cookies', 'browsing history', 'mouse movements', feeding a small gate labelled 'confident?'. Two branches leave the gate: 'confident you're human' goes straight through; 'unsure' opens a small grid of drawn picture squares. 'The click itself isn't the test' sits small at the top.

show.event: a drawn checkbox with 'I'm not a robot' draws in; the cursor ticks it on 'the "I'm not a robot" checkbox'
the click shrinks and three chips slide in behind it: cookies, browsing history, mouse movements, on 'signals like your cookies, your browsing history and your mouse movements'
the chips feed a gate 'confident?'; the 'confident' branch goes straight through, on 'you go straight through'
the 'unsure' branch opens a small grid of picture squares, on 'only if it's unsure does it ask you to pick pictures'

beats.note: Simple drawn checkbox. No reCAPTCHA branding, no real widget.

beats.narration_text: The next version, reCAPTCHA v3, shows no puzzle at all. It watches how each visitor behaves and gives a score between zero and one. A score close to zero means you're more likely a bot.

shot.visual_intent: A visitor's path (a short drawn line of a cursor moving across a plain page) is watched by a small eye shape; no puzzle appears. The eye feeds a semicircular dial marked 0 at the left end and 1 at the right end. The needle settles at an example spot near the 0 end; a tag 'closer to 0: more likely a bot' sits there. 'Illustrative score' reads small. The only numbers on screen are 0 and 1.

show.event: 'reCAPTCHA v3' lands as plain text; a plain page with a moving cursor path draws in and no puzzle appears, on 'shows no puzzle at all'
a small eye shape follows the cursor path on 'watches how each visitor behaves'
a dial marked 0 and 1 draws in and the needle swings to an example spot on 'gives a score between zero and one'
the needle settles near 0 and the tag 'closer to 0: more likely a bot' lands, on 'more likely a bot'

beats.note: Listen-check 'reCAPTCHA v3'. The needle position is an example, labelled illustrative; it is not a measured score.

beats.narration_text: Cloudflare moved away from puzzles too. Instead, your browser quietly solves small background challenges, and the system checks for signs of a real browser and human behaviour. Cloudflare reported that the CAPTCHAs it showed fell by ninety-one percent in a year, and the average check went from thirty-two seconds to about one.

shot.visual_intent: Left: a plain browser box quietly running three small background tasks (small gear shapes labelled 'small background challenges') while a tick for 'real browser?' and a tick for 'human behaviour?' appear beside it; no puzzle appears. Right: two plain figures. First a bar labelled 'CAPTCHAs shown' shrinks by 91%; then a stopwatch face whose hand drops from 32 seconds to about 1 second, with 'average check' beneath. No Cloudflare logo, no Cloudflare colours as branding; 'Cloudflare' appears as plain text only where it is spoken.

show.event: 'Cloudflare' appears as plain text; the plain browser box draws in with no puzzle
three small gears turn quietly inside the box on 'your browser quietly solves small background challenges'; two ticks follow, 'real browser?' and 'human behaviour?'
a bar of 'CAPTCHAs shown' shrinks by 91% on 'fell by ninety-one percent in a year'
a stopwatch hand drops from 32 seconds to about 1 second on 'from thirty-two seconds to about one'

beats.note: Listen-check Cloudflare. The 91% and 32 s to about 1 s figures are the Cloudflare post's own (about its Managed Challenge, not Turnstile by name); the narration does not say Turnstile and neither does the scene.

beats.narration_text: And there's a twist. Researchers at UC Irvine had fourteen hundred people solve fourteen thousand CAPTCHAs. On distorted text, people took nine to fifteen seconds and were right fifty to eighty-four percent of the time. Bots, from earlier studies, took under a second, with ninety-nine point eight percent accuracy.

shot.visual_intent: Plain header: '1,400 people, 14,000 CAPTCHAs' above a drawn distorted-text sample. Two rows, 'people' and 'bots (from earlier studies)'. Row 1, time: people 9 to 15 seconds as a long bar, bots under 1 second as a sliver. Row 2, accuracy: people 50 to 84 percent as a range band, bots 99.8 percent as a near-full bar. 'distorted text' labels the whole panel. The ranges are drawn as ranges, not single bars.

show.event: 'UC Irvine' appears as plain text; the header '1,400 people, 14,000 CAPTCHAs' lands on 'fourteen hundred people solve fourteen thousand CAPTCHAs'
the time row draws: people 9 to 15 seconds as a long bar, on 'nine to fifteen seconds'
the accuracy row draws: people as a band from 50 to 84 percent, on 'fifty to eighty-four percent of the time'
the bots' sliver under 1 second and the near-full 99.8 percent bar land, with 'from earlier studies' small beneath

beats.note: Listen-check UC Irvine. Figures are the paper's own (Table 3), drawn as ranges where the paper gives ranges.

beats.act: A HUNDRED PERCENT ON THE PICTURES
beats.narration_text: Image puzzles fell too. A team at ETH Zurich trained an AI image model that solved one hundred percent of Google's picture challenges, where earlier work solved sixty-eight to seventy-one percent. The same researchers found that the system relies heavily on cookies and browsing history to decide who's human. The picture alone was never the whole test.

shot.visual_intent: Left: a drawn picture grid with a bar below it that fills to 100 percent beside a shorter earlier bar marked 68 to 71 percent (as a band). Right: the same grid with two chips, 'cookies' and 'browsing history', feeding a small gate labelled 'who's human?', the chips drawn heavier than the grid. 'The picture alone was never the whole test' lands last as framing. ETH Zurich appears as plain text only. No mouse path, no claim that the system faked anything.

show.event: 'ETH Zurich' appears as plain text; a picture grid draws in and a bar fills to 100 percent, with an earlier band at 68 to 71 percent beside it, on 'one hundred percent' and 'sixty-eight to seventy-one'
two chips, cookies and browsing history, feed a gate 'who's human?' beside the grid, on 'relies heavily on cookies and browsing history'
the line 'The picture alone was never the whole test' lands

beats.note: Listen-check ETH Zurich. The earlier 'fake human signals' line was removed from the script; the scene shows the paper's finding about cookies and browsing history instead. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: So websites are changing what they check. They use scores instead of puzzles, and watch behaviour in the background. One Cloudflare leader argues for blocking bad behaviour rather than every bot. And companies are working on ways to verify which AI agents are allowed in.

shot.visual_intent: Four plain steps. A puzzle grid is replaced by a score dial; a small eye over a cursor path stays in the background; a shield at a gate stops a drawn robot labelled 'bad behaviour', with a small tag 'one Cloudflare leader argues' (plain text); a second drawn robot with a small tag 'verified' is checked at the gate, tagged 'companies are working on it'.

show.event: a puzzle grid slides away and a score dial takes its place on 'scores instead of puzzles'
a small eye follows a cursor path in the background on 'watch behaviour in the background'
a shield at a gate stops the robot labelled 'bad behaviour' under the small tag 'one Cloudflare leader argues', on 'blocking bad behaviour rather than every bot'
a second robot with a 'verified' tag is checked at the gate on 'verify which AI agents are allowed in'

beats.note: Drawn shapes only. The blocking-behaviour line is shown as one person's view, as the script now says; see FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: The traffic lights were never the whole test. A lot of it was how I moved. Puzzles are still around, but more and more, websites are moving from "prove you're human" to "show you behave like one."

the heading lands: show you behave like one
the closing line lands: from 'prove you're human' to 'show you behave like one'

beats.narration_text: Your turn. This week, count how many times a website asks if you're human, and notice when it lets you through without asking. Then paste this into Claude: Explain why a website showed me a "Verify you are human" page, what it might have checked in the background, and how you would tell a person from a bot without traffic lights.
